title: The Riot That Taught a Boy About Human Nature
book: The Blank Slate: The Modern Denial of Human Nature
author: Steven Pinker
wiifm: Are people shaped entirely by upbringing, or do we arrive with natures of our own? The answer changes how you hire, how you parent, how you nurse and how you design any system that people have to live inside. The Blank Slate is Steven Pinker's case that we are not infinitely moldable, and that admitting it is not dangerous. You will follow Pinker from a Montreal childhood during a police strike to the laboratories of Harvard and MIT, and you will also hear where his critics think he overreached.

ch.h: The night the police went home
b: Steven Arthur Pinker was born on the eighteenth of September 1954 in Montreal, into an English-speaking Jewish family. His father trained as a lawyer and worked as a sales representative, his mother became a school vice principal, and the household was full of argument and books. In his teens, like many of his generation, he flirted with anarchism and assumed that if you removed the police and the state, people would get along perfectly well.

Then, on the seventh of October 1969, the Montreal police went on strike. Within hours, as Pinker later described it, banks were robbed, shops were looted, fires were set and a police officer was shot dead in the confusion. By the evening the army had been called in.

Pinker was fifteen. He has said that this one day was enough to cure him of his anarchist views. People, it seemed, were not simply waiting for society to stop corrupting them. Remove the restraints, and something else came out. Three decades later he would build a whole book around that question.

The strike lasted only about sixteen hours, ending when the government passed emergency legislation that night. But its lesson stuck. Pinker later wrote that it was a vivid demonstration of how much ordinary peace depends on the expectation of consequences, an idea that runs through The Blank Slate and his later work on violence.
ch.cap: Fifteen-year-old Pinker watches Montreal burn during the strike

b: Pinker studied psychology at McGill University in Montreal and then went to Harvard, where he completed his doctorate in experimental psychology in 1979. He spent most of the 1980s and 1990s at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studying how children learn language, especially how they acquire regular and irregular verbs, why they say holded before they learn held.

Language shaped his view of human nature. Following Noam Chomsky, he became convinced that children could not learn something so intricate from scratch. They must come equipped with mental machinery designed for the job. His first popular book, The Language Instinct in 1994, argued exactly that, and How the Mind Works in 1997 extended the idea to the whole mind, drawing on evolutionary psychology.

One of his favourite pieces of evidence came from Nicaragua. In the late 1970s and 1980s deaf children brought together in new schools invented their own sign language, and the younger children who learned it made it richer and more grammatical than the older ones who had started it. To Pinker, this was a language instinct in action: children were not just copying, they were building.

By the late 1990s he had become one of the clearest science writers in the world. And he had noticed something odd. Among many intellectuals, the idea that people come with any innate nature at all seemed not just mistaken but morally suspect.
ch.cap: Deaf children in Nicaragua invent their own sign language

b: The Blank Slate, published in 2002, begins by naming three ideas that Pinker believes dominated modern thinking about people. The first is the blank slate itself, the doctrine, often linked to the philosopher John Locke, that the mind has no inherent structure and is written on entirely by experience. Locke actually used the image of white paper rather than a slate, but the idea is the same.

The second is the noble savage, associated loosely with Jean Jacques Rousseau, though he never used the phrase himself. It holds that humans are naturally peaceful and good, and are corrupted by society. The third is the ghost in the machine, a phrase the philosopher Gilbert Ryle coined in 1949 to mock the idea, descended from Descartes, that each of us has an immaterial soul that makes choices independently of biology.

Pinker argues that these three ideas were adopted partly because they seemed to protect cherished values. If people are blank, nobody is born inferior. If people are naturally good, then society can be perfected. If there is a ghost, then we have free will and responsibility. His project is to show that we can keep those values without the false science.

Pinker traces the blank slate into the twentieth century, through the behaviourist John B Watson, who boasted in the 1920s that he could take any healthy infant and train it to become any kind of specialist, from doctor to thief, whatever its talents or ancestry. Watson admitted he was going beyond the facts, but the boast captured a mood. Behaviourism, much of anthropology and parts of social science treated human nature as close to infinitely flexible.

He is not arguing that culture does not matter. His point is that culture and learning themselves depend on innate equipment. A blank slate could not learn anything at all, because it would have no way of deciding what to notice, what to ignore and how to generalise. Learning requires machinery designed to learn.
ch.cap: Blank slate, noble savage and ghost in the machine

b: Pinker then gathers evidence that the mind is not blank. He points to the anthropologist Donald Brown's list of human universals, features found in every documented culture, such as language, music, kinship terms, gossip, status, envy, rules about sex and words for emotions. If culture were infinitely variable, he asks, why do all cultures share so much?

He leans heavily on twin and adoption studies. Identical twins raised apart turn out to be strikingly similar in personality, intelligence and even political attitudes. Across many traits, roughly forty to fifty per cent of the variation between people in a given population can be linked to genetic differences. Pinker states these as laws of behavioural genetics, drawing on the psychologist Eric Turkheimer: all traits are partly heritable, the shared family environment matters less than you might expect, and a large part of the variation comes from neither, from chance and unique experience.

That last point surprises most people. Pinker cites Judith Rich Harris, whose 1998 book The Nurture Assumption argued that, beyond a basic level of care, parenting style has less effect on adult personality than we suppose, and that peers matter a great deal. This remains disputed, and later research suggests parents matter in some areas more than Harris allowed. But it shook the idea that children are simply moulded by home.

Pinker is careful to say that a ghost in the machine was never needed to explain choice. The brain itself, with its billions of neurons, is the thing that weighs options, imagines futures and makes decisions. To say that choice is physical is not to say that it is unreal, any more than saying a song is made of vibrations makes the music disappear.
ch.cap: Twins raised apart meet wearing identical clothes

b: The heart of the book is Pinker's answer to why people resist these findings. He names four fears, and takes each in turn.

The fear of inequality: if people differ by nature, does that justify discrimination? Pinker answers that equality is a moral principle, a commitment to treat people as individuals and judge them on their own merits, not a factual claim that everyone is identical. The fear of imperfectability: if human nature is fixed, is social progress impossible? No, he says, because human nature includes reason, empathy and the ability to make rules and agreements, which can be used to improve society.

The fear of determinism: if behaviour has biological causes, can anyone be held responsible? Pinker replies that responsibility is a practical tool that works because people respond to incentives, and that biological causes do not cancel it any more than environmental ones do. And the fear of nihilism: if we are evolved machines, does life lose meaning? He argues that meaning comes from our own experience and our relationships, which remain real whatever their origin.

Pinker adds that the opposite fear, that admitting human nature will lead to cruelty, has it backwards. The worst horrors of the twentieth century, he argues, often came from regimes that believed human nature could be remade entirely, and were willing to break people in the attempt.

Running underneath all four answers is a single move. Pinker separates facts from values. What people are like is a question for science. How we should treat each other is a question for ethics. Confusing the two, he argues, makes people deny inconvenient findings in order to protect decent values, when those values never depended on the findings in the first place.
ch.cap: Pinker's lantern holds back four looming fears

b: Pinker takes the noble savage on directly, and here the Montreal police strike returns. He gathers evidence from archaeology and anthropology that rates of violent death in many non-state societies were very high, often far higher than in modern states. Skeletons with arrowheads, fortified villages and ethnographic records of raiding all suggest that pre-state life was not usually peaceful.

He would develop this into a much bigger argument in The Better Angels of Our Nature in 2011, claiming that violence has declined over history. Critics have challenged both books on this point. Some anthropologists, such as Douglas Fry and R Brian Ferguson, argue that Pinker selected unusually violent societies, mixed very different kinds of evidence, and underestimated how peaceful many foragers were. The debate remains active.

He also revisits Margaret Mead's famous 1928 book Coming of Age in Samoa, which described a relaxed island culture free of adolescent turmoil and sexual jealousy. The anthropologist Derek Freeman later challenged it fiercely, arguing that Samoan society was in fact strict and often violent. Freeman's critique has its own critics, and the dispute still divides anthropologists, but for Pinker it shows how much people wanted the noble savage to be true.

His underlying claim, though, is more modest and harder to dispute: humans have the capacity for both violence and cooperation, and whether one or the other dominates depends heavily on institutions, incentives and norms. That night in Montreal, the potential for violence had always been there. The police strike simply removed the brakes.
ch.cap: A skull with an arrowhead lies below a fortified village

b: In the last part of the book Pinker applies his view to the most heated topics of his time: politics, violence, gender, children and the arts. On politics he suggests that left and right partly reflect different views of human nature. The tragic vision, as the economist Thomas Sowell called it, sees human nature as limited and in need of restraint by traditions and institutions. The utopian vision sees people as perfectible. Pinker thinks the science lends more support to the tragic vision, while accepting that progress is possible.

On gender he argues that some average psychological differences between men and women have partly biological roots, while insisting that averages say nothing about any individual and that discrimination is wrong regardless. This chapter has drawn some of the sharpest criticism, with scholars such as Cordelia Fine arguing that many claimed sex differences are smaller, more variable and more shaped by culture than Pinker suggests.

On children, he restates that genes and chance matter more and parenting style less than many believe. On the arts, he criticises modernist movements that rejected beauty and pattern, arguing that art speaks to an evolved human aesthetic.

He tells the story of David Reimer, a Canadian boy whose penis was destroyed in a botched circumcision in 1966. On the advice of the psychologist John Money, who believed gender identity was learned, he was raised as a girl. Money reported the case as a success. It was not. Reimer never felt like a girl, and as a teenager he learned the truth and lived the rest of his life as a man. His life ended tragically in 2004. To Pinker, the case showed the human cost of insisting that nature does not exist.
ch.cap: Raised as a girl, a boy finds himself

b: The Blank Slate was a bestseller and a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize, but it was also attacked from several sides, and it is fair to hear them.

Some critics argued that Pinker attacked a straw man. Very few serious scientists, they said, really believed the mind was entirely blank. The biologist H Allen Orr and the philosopher Simon Blackburn both made versions of this point. Others challenged the heritability figures. Heritability describes variation within a particular population and environment, not how fixed a trait is, and critics warned that it is easily misunderstood. Since 2002, large genetic studies have found that individual genes each have tiny effects, and that predicting behaviour from DNA is much harder than some hoped, though they broadly confirm that genes influence most traits.

Pinker's reply was that the blank slate rarely appears as an explicit scientific claim but often lurks as an assumption, in statements that gender or aggression are purely social constructions, and in hostile reactions to scientists who suggested otherwise. He recalls the biologist E O Wilson being doused with a jug of water at a scientific meeting in 1978 by protesters angry at his work on sociobiology.

Evolutionary psychology itself, on which the book leans, has been criticised for producing stories that are hard to test. Pinker has defended it vigorously. The fairest summary is that the book won the main argument, that human nature exists and matters, while many of its specific claims remain contested.
ch.cap: A protester pours water over E O Wilson in 1978

b: Pinker moved to Harvard in 2003 and has remained one of the most influential and argued-over public intellectuals in the world. The Blank Slate is still his most direct answer to the question raised that night in Montreal.

He also became a passionate defender of reason and science more widely, in Enlightenment Now in 2018 and Rationality in 2021. Both books carry the same theme as The Blank Slate. Human nature includes our weaknesses, our tribalism and our biases. It also includes the ability to recognise them and to build institutions, like science and law, that help us rise above them.

Its lasting message is that knowing human nature is not a threat but a tool. People come with tendencies: to seek status, favour kin, fear outsiders, cooperate when it pays, and reason their way to better rules. Systems built for imaginary blank people fail. Systems built for real ones, with their mixture of selfishness and decency, have a far better chance of working.

There is a personal note in this, too. The teenager who watched Montreal burn did not decide that people were wicked. He decided they were complicated, capable of both looting and rebuilding, and that a good society is one that makes the better choice the easier one.
ch.cap: Montreal rebuilds at dawn after the night of looting

take: Build rules and processes around how people actually behave, with incentives and safeguards, not around how you wish they would.
Treating people fairly is a moral commitment, not a claim that everyone is identical. Judge each person as an individual.
The Montreal strike showed how fast order can slip. Keep clear rules and checks in place, even when everyone seems trustworthy.
People arrive with dispositions. Hire and place staff to suit their strengths, rather than expecting training to remake them.
Biological causes do not cancel accountability. Consistent consequences shape behaviour because people respond to them.
Harris argued peers matter enormously. Pay attention to the culture of the groups your team or children spend time in.
Heritability describes populations, not individuals. Never use an average to predict or limit a particular person.
recall: What event changed Pinker's view of human nature as a teenager?
The Montreal police strike of the seventh of October 1969, when looting, arson and violence broke out within hours. It cured him of the idea that people would naturally get along without restraint.
What are the three doctrines Pinker challenges?

The blank slate, that the mind has no innate structure; the noble savage, that humans are naturally good and corrupted by society; and the ghost in the machine, an immaterial soul independent of biology.

The fears of inequality, imperfectability, determinism and nihilism. He argues each can be answered without denying human nature, for example that equality is a moral principle rather than a factual claim of sameness.

All traits are partly heritable, the shared family environment has less effect than expected, and much variation comes from chance and unique experience. Pinker draws on twin studies, Turkheimer and Judith Rich Harris.

Critics such as H Allen Orr and Simon Blackburn say Pinker attacked a straw man, since few scientists held a fully blank view. Others challenge his use of heritability, his claims about pre-state violence, his treatment of sex differences and the testability of evolutionary psychology.

stories: The day the police went home

In 1969 Steven Pinker was a fifteen-year-old in Montreal who, like many of his generation, flirted with anarchism: remove the police and the state, and people would get along fine. On the seventh of October that year, the Montreal police went on strike. Within hours, banks were robbed, shops looted, fires set, and a police officer was shot dead in the confusion. By evening the army had been called in, and the strike ended that night after about sixteen hours. Pinker says that one day cured him of anarchism. Decades later he built The Blank Slate around the question it raised: what is in us when the brakes come off?
The children who invented a language

In Nicaragua in the late 1970s and 1980s, deaf children who had grown up isolated were brought together in new schools for the first time. Nobody taught them a full sign language, so they built one themselves out of the gestures they brought from home. Then something remarkable happened. Younger children who picked it up from the older ones did not simply copy it. They made it richer, faster and more grammatical than the children who had started it. For Pinker, it was a language instinct caught in the act: children are not blank slates waiting to be written on, they arrive with machinery built to construct language.

In 1978 the Harvard biologist E O Wilson was about to speak at a meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. Three years earlier his book Sociobiology had suggested that some human social behaviour had evolutionary roots. Protesters who saw that idea as dangerous rushed the stage and poured a jug of water over his head. Wilson, the story goes, dried himself off and gave his talk. Pinker tells it in The Blank Slate as evidence that the blank slate was not only an abstract academic position. It was a belief people felt so strongly about that suggesting otherwise could get a distinguished scientist soaked in public.
biz: Keep the brakes on, even with good people

The Montreal strike showed how quickly behaviour changes when checks disappear, even among ordinary decent people. That is not a reason to distrust your team; it is a reason to design for real humans under pressure. This week, confirm three controls exist and are used: a second person checks every case before it goes to a lender, a sample of recorded calls is reviewed against a short quality checklist each week, and any change to ad copy or a financial promotion is approved before it runs. Measure the share of files checked, the errors caught, and how many complaints trace back to something a check would have spotted.
Judge the person, not the average

Pinker insists that averages say nothing about any individual, and that treating people fairly is a moral commitment, not a claim that everyone is the same. Ad platforms and lead scoring work on averages, by age, area or device, and it is easy for those shortcuts to become unfair treatment of a real person. This week, list every rule you use to prioritise or drop leads in both businesses and ask of each: is it based on this person's actual circumstances, or on a group they belong to? Under Consumer Duty, check outcomes by customer group, such as how long vulnerable clients wait, so no group is quietly served worse.
connects: Machiavelli's view that rulers must assume people will behave badly unless restrained is an early form of what Pinker, after Thomas Sowell, calls the tragic vision of human nature.
Adam Smith, like Pinker, designs for people as they are, letting self-interest be channelled by markets and institutions instead of hoping to remake human nature.
Ericsson's argument that deliberate practice outweighs innate talent offers a useful counterweight to Pinker's emphasis on what we are born with.
recap:
Begin in Montreal in nineteen sixty nine, with a fifteen year old called Steven Pinker who is rather taken with anarchism. Get rid of the police and the state, he thinks, and people will get along perfectly well. Then, one October morning, the Montreal police go on strike. Within hours banks are robbed, shops are looted, fires are set, and a police officer is shot dead. By evening the army is on the streets. One day is enough to cure him of his anarchism.

He goes on to study how children learn language, at Harvard and at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and becomes convinced that children could not learn something so intricate from scratch. In Nicaragua, deaf children brought together for the first time invent a sign language of their own, and the youngest make it richer than the ones who started it. Minds, he concludes, come with machinery built in. And he notices something odd: many intellectuals treat that idea as not just wrong, but dangerous.

So in two thousand and two he publishes The Blank Slate. The first big idea is that three old beliefs shaped modern thinking: that the mind starts blank, that people are naturally good until society spoils them, and that a ghost inside us makes our choices free of biology.

The second idea is the evidence against the blank slate. Every known culture shares features such as music, gossip, status and envy. Identical twins raised apart turn out strikingly alike. Genes influence almost every trait, though each gene does very little, and chance plays a big part too.

The third idea is the heart of the book: the four fears. People worry that human nature means inequality, that progress is impossible, that nobody is responsible, and that life has no meaning. Pinker answers each one by separating facts from values. Treating people equally is a moral choice, not a claim that everyone is identical. Human nature includes reason and empathy, so improvement is possible.

The fourth idea is that our capacity for violence and for cooperation are both real, and which wins depends on institutions, incentives and norms.

The fifth is fair warning. Critics say Pinker attacked a straw man, overstated sex differences and the violence of early societies, and that heritability is easily misunderstood. The main argument, that human nature exists and matters, has largely held.

The teenager who watched Montreal burn did not decide that people were wicked. He decided they were complicated. Here is the line to remember: systems built for imaginary blank people fail, and systems built for real people, with all their mixture of selfishness and decency, have a chance of working.
